stories.title: Scrapping pensions triple lock 'morally wrong', says union boss
stories.summary: Andy Burnham wants to outline his ideas for a free-at-the-point-of-use social care system in his first speech to Labour conference as prime minister.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Union boss Sharon Graham has been an outspoken critic of Labour governments in the past

Published 29 September 2026, 09:30 BST

Unite the Union general secretary Sharon Graham has warned the prime minister that scrapping the pensions triple lock would be "morally wrong", as Andy Burnham prepares to deliver his first speech to Labour conference as PM.

Burnham told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg that he wants to use his speech to set out his "vision" to introduce an NHS-style social care system, free at the point of use.

There is growing speculation about how such a care system could be funded, including removing the pensions triple lock in the future.

Labour's deputy leader Lucy Powell told BBC Breakfast the party is committed to the triple lock, which was in the party's 2024 manifesto.

The triple lock, which has been in place for 16 years, means state pensions rise every April by at least 2.5% or in line with the highest of prices or earnings.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Graham said axing the triple lock risked repeating the unpopular removal of the Winter Fuel Allowance under previous prime minister Sir Keir Starmer.

"Instead of going to try and pick the pocket of pensioners, we need to move over to the other side of the equation and think about things like wealth taxes way before we try to stop something like the triple lock," she said.

"Going to a group of people who are getting around £12,500 a year in order to pay for it [social care], to take away their security, is wrong - I think its morally wrong," she added, highlighting how current pensions are the lowest of the G7 countries.

On Tuesday morning, Powell said the lock was a manifesto commitment, and asked whether it would stay in place until the next election, she said: "I can absolutely assure your viewers watching this that we are committed to the triple lock, it's in our manifesto.

"The triple lock is really delivering for pensioners right now: over the course of this parliament it's set to increase the value of the state pension by around about £2,000 a year - significant uplifts to the state pension."

Speaking to the BBC, Burnham set out his proposal for a new social care system to help people live more independently. He said social care in England is "as unfair as American healthcare, where the most vulnerable in society can lose everything, they can be wiped out" and indicated "nothing is off the table at this moment in time" on funding.

Unlike the NHS, social care is not free at the point of use. In England and Northern Ireland, people with savings worth more than £23,250 are not entitled to help with care costs from their council.

In Wales and Scotland, different rules apply in terms of eligibility.

Alan Milburn, the former Labour minister who is currently leading an independent review into young people and work for the government, has said scrapping the triple lock to fund social care is "the sort of call" the prime minister is "prepared to make".

In the BBC's Political Thinking podcast, Milburn was asked if Burnham's new social care plans could be funded by getting rid of the triple lock, he responded that Burnham was "exactly the sort of person who can take the big decisions".

He said: "Andy is absolutely right about this - the social care system is broken... That is going to be a really big call.

"But it's the sort of call that I've got no doubt - from everything, and every conversation I've been in with him - it's the sort of call that he is prepared to make."

Burnham is also expected to announce a new government body to invest in Britain's electricity grid, branded Great British Grid , in his speech.

How can we fix our pricing crisis? Economic sociologist Lindsay Owens urges tough new rules – and a consumer uprising

“R epeat after me: it’s not my fault, it’s not my fault, it’s not my fault.” That’s the message to frustrated US shoppers in Gouged: The End of a Fair Price – and What That Means for Your Wallet by Lindsay Owens, economic sociologist and head of the Groundwork Collaborative, a progressive Washington thinktank.

Consumer rage is rising and no wonder – we are all living through the “reinvention of the rip-off”, Owens told the Guardian, an experience that is undermining Americans’ trust in the economy. Nothing short of a consumer uprising and a slate of tough new rules is going to fix the problem, she believes.

The book concludes with a “ shoppers’ bill of rights ” that lays out how local and federal governments could write rules to fix the problem: ban companies from using shared software to coordinate prices, it urges, and require AI “shopping assistants” to act in consumers’ best interest, not steer them to higher-price items, among other moves.

“A cost of living crisis is the right time to build the constituency for a revived consumer movement in this country,” Owens says.

The following interview was compiled from several conversations and edited and condensed for clarity.

Why did you write Gouged?

Right around the time that America started experiencing rising inflation and cost of living in 2021, I started to realize that there was something else going on besides just high prices. The way companies were talking about pricing was starting to shift.

Their costs were going up but they weren’t too worried about it. They were planning to pass all of their rising costs along to us, and they were pretty bullish about gilding the lily and going for more.

In an economy with competitive pricing, that shouldn’t happen, right?

I started to see a little bit of a breadcrumb trail: “Oh, these companies are bullish because they have a plan for this, right?” They have some new techniques and technologies they’re planning to deploy, they have some new partnerships, they’ve been buying up AI pricing companies … they were ready for this moment.

What actually changed inside corporate boardrooms? Cost-cutting hit bone. I cut my teeth in academia and the Senate studying the ruthless form of American capitalism that’s centered around it: bust unions and keep wages down, pass Nafta and outsource labor, bring in the bean counters from the big four accounting firms and ask: “How do we limit our regulatory costs?”

Low prices were part of that part of capitalism.

But there’s been a shift toward the revenue side of the ledger that includes getting better on price hiking. That’s easier to do when there’s less competition, but it’s also the result of new technologies.

Gouged details data -mining companies unknown to the average consumer, like EverSight, Kronos, Plexure. How important have they been to the “gouging” problem US consumers are facing?

Hugely important. Their dossiers contain thousands of data points and inferences about consumers, including their age, income, health, religion and even partisan affiliation.

Virtually no one evades data brokers’ grasp. One data broker claims to have data profiles on roughly 95% of adults.

With these troves of personal data in hand, retailers increasingly rely on outside consultants and AI startups who specialize in the “art and science behind pricing decisions”. They run experiments on consumers – and even personalize prices to each consumer’s pain point.

Should these companies exist in an economy that’s also fair to workers and consumers?

Profit maximization is not intrinsically problematic. In a competitive marketplace, companies would have to compete on price and quality in order to win over consumers, resulting in better products and better deals. However, as competition disappears and the law struggles to keep pace, new technologies and newer, more brazen methods of corporate profiteering erode the basic social contract between shoppers and retailers.

Companies whose sole purpose is to harvest consumer data would probably cease to exist if Congress had passed adequate privacy protections. Companies should not get a gold star for refusing to gouge customers; they should be required not to.

There’s a lot of telling history in this book, like the lightbulb that has been burning in California for 120 years , and how manufacturers banded together to make sure they never lasted that long again. Yet we’re still surprised by “planned obsolescence”. Have modern US consumers just been too naive?

I think we all have a sense that this is going on and something has shifted, but we don’t fully appreciate how systematic and how purposeful this is.

Whether it’s making the jar of Skippy peanut butter concave, degrading product quality, locking you out of something you bought, forcing you to pay top dollar for parts and repair – all of that is really baked into how companies operate these days.

I don’t think Americans are naive. But every 10 or 20 years we need to have a conversation about what we’re owed as consumers and shoppers. It’s time to update the rules.

How are American shoppers doing right now?

I think American shoppers are exhausted. High prices make shopping pretty treacherous.

The amount of basics Americans are putting on credit cards, the amount of Americans who are using things like “ buy now, pay later ” shows how difficult it is.

Adding insult to injury is the increasingly opaque manipulative and volatile way that corporate America does pricing.

This reinvention of the rip-off that we’re all living through has undermined trust in one of the major ways we participate in the economy.

Comparison shopping is almost impossible now. Trying to get a refund is a three-day battle with a chatbot, and even if you think you won, you’d better remember to check with your bank to make sure they actually follow through.

Where are we in the current inflation and rising cost cycle?

I don’t even think we’re even at the halfway point. This is something I’ve been saying since 2022. Every time I was on the Hill, I was screaming at the Biden administration to focus more on prices and cost of living.

This is a once-in-50-year period of high inflation. Something has completely changed in our culture and our economy, in our politics, and you have to be responsive to it.

You wrote Gouged before the US and Israel attacks on Iran, which have ramped up inflation.

Yes. I do talk in the book about Trump’s trade war, and its impact on prices. The Iran war is similar. Most Americans do understand how gas prices ripple through the whole economy.

The fog of war, the fog of crisis, is really powerful. It makes it so that Americans have a hard time discerning which piece of the price increase is indeed because of import costs, and which is companies gilding the lily. Buckle up.

You expect companies to take advantage of the war?

Absolutely.

What about your personal shopping? How are you and your family navigating this situation?

The first thing I will say is I am not the “points guy” for e-commerce. I, like you, am being screwed by these companies.

Most Americans are balancing trying to get a good deal with figuring out how much time they could possibly spend on not getting ripped off.

So I updated how I comparison-shop. I look at brick and mortar, on the app, logged in, logged out. I try not to buy in-app.

I run experiments. Call your friends and say: “What price are you seeing?” My husband and I sit in bed with our laptops open, figuring out which of us gets the better deal. Whoever gets the better deal buys the plane tickets.

One thing I often hear from readers is “nothing is ever going to change” – a sort of pessimism about reforming the system.

I do think the deck is stacked against us and we have our work cut out. It feels like Whac-A-Mole – you get a win in one city, you find out your bill is vetoed in another.

[Colorado governor] Jared Polis vetoed surveillance pricing legislation. We’re still waiting for [New York governor] Kathy Hochul to sign a bill that passed there.

But when Americans find out that companies are partnering with AI companies to spy on you and figure out how to take your last three pennies for every item in your grocery cart, they get pretty ticked off.

I think the optimism I have is the sort of public anger, and, frankly, the groundswell of public conversation around this.

The Federal Trade Commission is sorting through about 1,000 comments from Americans about surveillance pricing regulation.

Wendy’s had to cry “uncle” and say they wouldn’t do surge pricing on their electronic menu board. Delta cried “uncle”, and so did Instacart two weeks after Groundwork exposed their algorithmic pricing experiments.

I think all of that is a really important part about how we stick the genie back in the bottle, combined with legislative activity.

If Democrats take the House and Senate, there’s a long list of things they are expected to address related to the Trump administration, national security et cetera. Where should this be on the priority list?

The top issue for the American people, and it has been this way since 2022, is prices and the cost of living. Anything that takes on the economy is going to be top of the list.

The only that could shift could be rising concern about AI – and a lot of the most sinister nefarious and opaque pricing practices that corporate America is using are powered by AI.

We’re seeing interest from Republicans as well. I testified in front of [Missouri senator] Josh Hawley on this a couple weeks ago, at his request, as a majority witness, which has never happened to me before.

You ask readers to repeat “It’s not your fault” three times before they try to confront this new landscape. Why?

From the bottom of my heart, I don’t believe it should be Americans’ job to duck and dodge and beat the machine. The most dystopian version of this world is one in which there’s a “points guy” for everything.

Outsmarting price-gouging on your own is like trying to solve climate change by yourself.

Gougers are always reinventing themselves, always figuring out newer, more cunning ways to stay one step ahead. And all that effort eats up one of your most precious resources: time. Companies know this – and they are banking on it.

What are you hoping to change, near term?

It’s been a really long time since the consumer laws have been updated. I do think e-commerce and agentic commerce begs a new type of policy regime.

This year alone, there are 90 pieces of legislation throughout the country, in states and cities to try to curtail algorithmic price fixing. A cost of living crisis is the right time to build the constituency for a revived consumer movement in this country.

Chancellor sets out measures to support jobs and growth in conference speech but vows fiscal discipline in budget

Analysis: Healey offers upbeat vision but little light on how to pay for it

Average price of diesel on UK forecourts reaches all-time high

John Healey has signalled Labour will stage a fresh attempt at welfare reform as he pledged to put fiscal discipline at the core of next month’s budget, alongside measures to inject hope into Britain’s economy.

In his first speech as chancellor to the Labour conference , Healey warned that next month’s highly anticipated tax-and-spending event would need to take into account a challenging global backdrop.

Setting out measures to support jobs and growth, the chancellor announced a new local apprenticeship service, to be led by mayors, targeted at young people to deliver “thousands more apprenticeships” across the country.

However, he also gave the clearest indication yet that job support would be accompanied by changes to the welfare system designed to incentivise employment while curbing a soaring benefits bill.

Rolling the pitch to avoid a repeat of the welfare rebellion that forced his predecessor, Rachel Reeves, into a costly U-turn, Healey argued Labour had a “moral duty” to overhaul the system to encourage people to find a job.

“Our social security system must always be there for those who can never work. But for everyone else, benefits should be a bridge to work, to wider participation, to a better life, not a trap that people can’t escape,” he said. “And, conference, it is simply not progressive to allow a bigger and bigger benefits bill and a system which offers an income but doesn’t offer a future. So, once again, as a Labour government it falls to us to act.”

Insisting he would balance the books while fleshing out Andy Burnham’s plans to strengthen “growth in every postcode”, Healey said he and the prime minister were in lockstep in their commitment to balance the books.

“That commitment is so important. There is nothing progressive about losing control because it’s always working people who pay for it,” he said.

Against a backdrop of jitters in financial markets as the Iran war rattles the global economy, the UK government’s borrowing costs have risen to the highest levels for almost two decades.

Economists have warned that the chancellor could be forced to increase taxes or cut spending in response to rising pressures. However, with Burnham having promised to stick to Labour’s manifesto promise not to raise income tax, national insurance or VAT, investors view benefits reform as a totemic issue that could help the prime minister to demonstrate his commitment to balancing the books.

Since he replaced Keir Starmer this summer, Burnham has signalled that Labour remains willing to overhaul welfare, amid predictions that the overall cost of pensions and welfare benefits could reach £409bn by 2030.

In a speech aiming to strike a balance between promising to fund the new prime minister’s priorities and committing to fiscal discipline, Healey drew a comparison with the 1990s when he was an adviser to Gordon Brown.

Wearing a red tie that he had lent to Brown, then chancellor, to wear for a Labour conference speech in Bournemouth more than two decades ago, he said the money New Labour had in the 1990s “is simply not there now”.

Teeing up a tough budget on 28 October, in which Burnham has warned “difficult decisions” will need to be taken , Healey said the government needed to hold firm on its main fiscal rule requiring day-to-day spending to be matched by revenues by 2030.

Rain Newton-Smith, the chief executive of the business lobby group the CBI, said: “The speech sent many of the right signals. The budget now needs to turn them into action if we are to fundamentally change firms’ willingness to invest, take a chance on a young person, and scale a business here in the UK.”

Healey sought to draw a distinction between Labour’s approach and that of the Conservatives, saying Britain was suffering from the “reckless actions” the Tories had taken since 2010. He accused Reform UK of prioritising the interests of “dodgy” billionaire donors, saying Nigel Farage was “Liz Truss with a bitcoin account”.

Healey’s local apprenticeships announcement comes as ministers await recommendations from two reviews of the welfare system expected to be published this autumn – on young people by Alan Milburn, and on a key disability benefit by the Timms panel.

Milburn, a former Labour cabinet minister, has signalled that changes to welfare would be central to his recommendations, alongside measures to boost access to job support, education and training opportunities.

Aiming to strike a balance between a message of fiscal discipline and an upbeat approach, Healey used his conference speech to argue that his budget would inject hope into the economy.

The chancellor said actions would be taken to devolve power to regional mayors, alongside measures to support young people to find work and to reinvigorate business confidence. Healey also said he would allocate £6bn from the government’s defence investment plan to contracts for British shipyards, as part of a project to reindustrialise Britain.

“Let’s bring back hope to Britain. For the next generation of young people. For a new age of industrialisation. For growth made here, by British firms and British workers,” he said.

stories.title: UK tries to stop Trump's diesel export ban
stories.summary: John Healey said the government is in talks with the US over Donald Trump's threat to stop exports.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Chancellor John Healey

Published 28 September 2026

The UK is in talks with US authorities over a potential stoppage of diesel exports and has started preparing for a ban, Chancellor John Healey has told BBC News.

Diesel prices in the UK reached a new high on Monday due to supply pressures springing from the US-Israel conflict with Iran and Russia's war with Ukraine.

Fuel prices are rising globally and US President Donald Trump has threatened to ban diesel exports, stating at the weekend: "We're thinking about it very seriously."

Healey, who admitted that UK diesel prices are "extreme", said the government was in discussions with the US, adding: "We're also making the provision that we may need to and we have our own stocks in the UK."

Speaking on the sidelines of the annual Labour Party Conference in Liverpool, Healey said: "We work very closely with the Americans.

"In the end, we're also working with the Americans where we can try and put in place what will solve this, or at least significantly ease it, which would be a diplomatic settlement [and] an end to the fighting with Iran."

The UK depends on the US for around a third of its diesel imports and a ban would send prices even higher.

US sources suggest that Trump is considering a ban to attempt to bring down prices for domestic consumers ahead of the critical midterm elections.

The White House said no official policy announcements have been made, adding that Trump wants to see prices at the pump fall and "is evaluating all the options on the table".

In the UK, the average price for a litre of diesel reached 199.33p on Monday, according to the RAC motoring organisation, surpassing a previous high of 199.09p in June 2022 after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Petrol prices are also still rising, with a litre currently costing 174.23p.

Over the past seven months, the Iran war has severely disrupted the production and transportation of wholesale oil across the region, causing the price of fuels made from oil to surge.

The RAC said diesel prices had entered "uncharted territory" and served as a reminder of "just how exposed the UK is to events occurring far away".

Healey said he was "very aware" of these cost of living pressures as he prepared what he called a "breathing space" Budget on 28 October.

A freeze on fuel duty, first implemented by the Conservative government in 2022, is due to expire at the end of the year. Duty is scheduled to increase by 3p in January and a further 2p in March.

Healey said: "Fundamentally, what we need is a settlement in the Middle East. We need an easing of the pressure of costs on business, the costs on households and on ordinary families that we see at the pumps in the most extreme level today for diesel."

stories.body:
David Perdue’s remarks come after a Taiwanese minister spoke of the ‘severe’ military threat posed by Beijing to the self-ruled island

Donald Trump offered to sell weapons to China while hosting its leader, Xi Jinping, last week, the US ambassador to China said on Sunday.

David Perdue told Fox News on Sunday: “President Trump continues to say, hey, we sell arms to other people around the world. He actually asked President Xi, would he like to buy some at one point.”

On Monday, Chinese state media praised the “extraordinary level of courtesy” that Trump had shown Xi on the Chinese leader’s visit to Washington .

The extraordinary claim came during an interview about US policy on Taiwan, which has been waiting for months for Trump to approve a new arms sales ⁠package worth $14bn (£10.5bn), after a record multibillion-dollar deal was announced in December last year.

Trump’s level of commitment to protecting Taiwan has previously been questioned . At a meeting with Xi in Beijing in May, ⁠Trump said he was keeping the $14bn Taiwan arms sales package in abeyance, describing it as a “very good negotiating chip” in dealings with China.

Washington has long maintained a strategically ambiguous stance on whether it would defend Taiwan in the event of an invasion. But under the decades-old Taiwan Relations Act, it is required to provide Taipei with sufficient military equipment to defend itself.

Beijing has repeatedly said it “resolutely opposes” Washington’s arms sales to the island democracy, which it regards as a breakaway province, despite never having ruled it, and has not renounced the use of force to take it. During their Washington meeting last week, Xi urged Trump to oppose “Taiwan independence”, according to a readout from the official Chinese news agency Xinhua.

After Perdue’s interview, the White House told the New York Times the US had no plans to sell arms to China , while the state department said: “US law prohibits arms sales to China and there is no offer or plan to sell arms to China.”

China is a net exporter of weapons. Of the arms that it does import, most come from Russia, but the volume is rapidly falling thanks to advances in China’s own military manufacturing capacity. China’s arms imports fell by 72% between 2021 and 2025 compared with the previous five years, according to data from the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute.

Before the interview, the Taiwanese deputy foreign minister, Chen Ming-chi, spoke of the severe military threat China posed.

“Taiwan faces a severe situation in the Taiwan strait. Even though China’s economy is declining, it continues investing more resources into building military capacity. Under ‌this context, the US very much understands our defence needs,” he told reporters in Taipei.

On Sunday, a Taiwanese official, Shen Yu-chung, also pushed back on what he said was an attempt by Beijing to “falsely claim that the Chinese Communist party and the US were allies” in the second world war. A fact sheet released by the White House after the Trump-Xi summit had said China and the US “fought side by side to win” in the war.

China’s government during the second world war was the Republic of China led by Chiang Kai-shek. Chiang’s government fled to Taiwan in 1949 after losing the Chinese civil war to the communists, who established the People’s Republic of China in 1949.

In recent years Taiwan has sought to emphasise its history of fighting alongside western democratic allies as it hopes to bolster international support against aggression from Beijing.

Trump ​has not mentioned the sale ‌since last week’s summit, saying ‌only on Saturday that Xi understands his position on Taiwan.

Perdue told CNBC ​on Friday that there had been ​no change in Taiwan policy by Trump, including on arms ​sales.

The giant pandas, Ping Ping and Fu Shuang, will be hosted at Atlanta zoo. Beijing dispatched the first panda pair to the US in 1972 following President Richard Nixon’s landmark visit to China. It uses the animals to indicate satisfaction or displeasure with other nations. But it also charges heftily for their lease: reportedly, around $1m a year per pair. Americans’ views of China have warmed from a pandemic nadir, but are unlikely to be shifted much by two animals, however charming. These days they are more of a token gesture than a striking symbol.
